name: Earsdon Sword Dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A seasoned Northumbrian dancer with a deep respect for the mining heritage and a focus on precision and speed.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance company formed around 1800 in Earsdon, Northumberland.
It established a formal relationship with the Dukes of Northumberland in 1829, performing annually at Alnwick Castle.
on_screen: Map: England · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally performed during the Christmas season, specifically for the Dukes of Northumberland.
It is a display of community identity and historical mining culture.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Five dancers form a circle using flexible two-handled swords.
They perform intricate weaving figures without releasing the swords, ending with the formation of a 'nut' or star.
The movement is fast and requires precise coordination.
Watch for The Nut.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: A very tight circle that moves as a single unit; requires minimal floor space but high vertical clearance for jumps.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Royal Earsdon Sword Dancers are the primary custodians of this specific tradition.
Earsdon is a specific variant of the North East rapper sword dance tradition, distinguished by its 'Royal' status and specific Alnwick Castle connection.
The tradition has been continuous since the early 19th century, documented by Cecil Sharp in 1911.

chapters.title: First steps
chapters.goal: Master the rapper grip and circle movement

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 — First steps. Today: Master the rapper grip and circle movement.
Level: beginner. Difficulty of the dance overall: advanced.
Your instructor: A seasoned Northumbrian dancer with a deep respect for the mining heritage and a focus on precision and speed.
on_screen: Instructor front view, name of the chapter, the three things you will learn

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright and compact to allow for tight circular weaving.
Hands remain low, gripping the handles and tips of the flexible swords to form a continuous chain.
Relatively stable, with most movement occurring in the legs and through the weaving of the arms.
on_screen: Instructor front then side view; freeze-frame on validated posture

scenes.title: Count and rhythm
narration: Count: 1-2-3, 4-5-6 (six subdivisions grouped in two; practice pulse only). The meter is 6/8 or 4/4.
Rhythm pattern: Rapid, driving jigs or hornpipes.
Clap it first, then step it in place.
on_screen: Counts on screen, flashing on the beat
Metronome at 77 bpm
scenes.music: lesson_slow (clicks only until the step lands)

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Form a circle of five dancers
Step 2: Each dancer grasps the handle of their own sword and the tip of the sword to their left
Footwork from the sources: Rapid rhythmic stepping, often described as a form of clog dancing or 'shuffling' in time with the music.
Drill: Holding the handle and tip correctly
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen
scenes.counts: 1-2-3, 4-5-6 (six subdivisions grouped in two; practice pulse only)

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Perform rhythmic stepping (clog-style) in place
Step 4: Execute weaving figures (under and over swords) while maintaining the circle
Drill: Moving in a circle while maintaining tension
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo
scenes.counts: 1-2-3, 4-5-6 (six subdivisions grouped in two; practice pulse only)

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Basic rhythmic stepping in place
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Releasing the sword grip during figures; losing the rhythmic timing which can lead to entanglement.
